identification.summary: Ferocious Kitten is the name Kaspersky gave to an Iran-based espionage actor. Kaspersky says it has run surveillance against Persian-speaking individuals inside Iran since at least 2015 [S1][S2]. The group uses Persian-language Office decoy documents with malicious macros to install a custom Windows implant, MarkiRAT [S1][S2][S3]. MarkiRAT records keystrokes and clipboard content, uploads and downloads files, and runs arbitrary commands. Some variants hijack the Telegram and Chrome applications to stay persistent [S2][S4]. In July 2026 Recorded Future linked a new cluster, TAG-182, to MarkiRAT distribution through fake VPN and media-player apps. It cited tradecraft overlaps with Ferocious Kitten but did not assess an organizational link [S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky traced MarkiRAT activity back to at least 2015 [S1][S2]. The actor became publicly known in June 2021 after a lure document uploaded to VirusTotal in March 2021 was highlighted on Twitter [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft has no name for this actor: 'Ferocious Kitten' does not appear in Microsoft's public naming map as retrieved on 2026-10-15 [S8]. MITRE tracks the group as G0137 and lists BITSAdmin and MarkiRAT as its software [S7]. Kaspersky says some TTPs resemble those of Domestic Kitten (C2 domains reused for years) and Rampant Kitten (Telegram execution hijacking and KeePass data theft). These are TTP similarities, not shared attribution [S1][S4]. Recorded Future's TAG-182 is a separate cluster with overlapping tooling. Keep it distinct from Ferocious Kitten [S6].

attribution.sponsor: Iran (vendor assessment). Kaspersky describes the actor as appearing to be based in Iran and conducting domestic surveillance [S1][S4]. Recorded Future assesses that the related TAG-182 cluster is almost certainly an element of Iran's state surveillance apparatus [S6].
attribution.confidence: Kaspersky's assessment rests on victimology and on similarity to other Iran-focused surveillance actors, and its reporting names no sponsoring Iranian organization [S1][S2]. Recorded Future says its TAG-182/Ferocious Kitten overlaps support an operational connection, but more evidence is needed to judge whether the two clusters are organizationally linked [S6]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Persian-language lures that depict anti-regime protests or resistance camps [S2]; payloads built for software popular in Iran (Telegram, Psiphon) [S2][S3]; long-term C2 reuse and Telegram hijacking similar to Domestic Kitten and Rampant Kitten [S1][S4]; overlapping BITS job strings, file-naming patterns and C2 configurations between TAG-182 and historical MarkiRAT activity [S6].

objectives: Domestic surveillance of Persian speakers, especially people tied to opposition or anti-regime activity, including theft of credentials, keystrokes, clipboard content and files [S1][S2][S3]. Recorded Future assesses that TAG-182 also targets Iranians abroad [S6].

sectors: Users of censorship-circumvention tools (Psiphon, VPN apps) and Telegram
regions: Iranian diaspora / anti-government movements abroad (TAG-182, per Recorded Future) [S6]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky's victim set is Persian-speaking individuals who appear to be in Iran [S1]. Lures pose as images or videos of protests or resistance camps against the Iranian government [S2]. TAG-182 promotes its malicious downloads through Instagram posts and staged websites [S6]. No government, military or DIB victims are reported in the cited sources.

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spearphishing Office documents with malicious macros, disguised as images or videos [S2][S7]. MarkiRAT records keystrokes and clipboard content, transfers files and runs commands [S2]. Picus also lists screenshots, file-system searches for target file types and credential stores, and staged exfiltration over HTTP(S) [S9]. Some MarkiRAT variants hijack the Telegram and Chrome launchers to stay persistent [S2][S4]. One variant is a backdoored build of the Psiphon circumvention VPN [S3][S4]. The group uses Windows BITS (BITSAdmin) for downloads [S7][S6] and file masquerading such as right-to-left override [S7]. Kaspersky saw signs of Android implants (APK/DEX files hosted on C2) but obtained no samples [S4]. In 2026 TAG-182 spread MarkiRAT through fake Android apps posing as VPNs and media players, such as 'Pis2ray VPN', 'YEPlayer' and 'YEMPlayer', promoted mainly on Instagram [S6]. Secondary vendor write-ups say the group exploited MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 to deliver a PowerShell stealer [S9]. That claim is not confirmed in SafeBreach's primary reporting (see gaps) [S5].

campaigns.name: MarkiRAT surveillance operations begin
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky traces MarkiRAT activity against Persian speakers in Iran back to at least 2015.

campaigns.name: Lure document surfaces publicly
campaigns.summary: A lure document is uploaded to VirusTotal and highlighted on Twitter, prompting Kaspersky's investigation.

campaigns.name: Kaspersky exposes Ferocious Kitten
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky publishes its report on six years of covert surveillance in Iran. It describes MarkiRAT, Telegram/Chrome hijacking, the backdoored Psiphon build, and signs of Android implants.

campaigns.name: PowerShortShell / CVE-2021-40444 campaign (disputed link)
campaigns.summary: SafeBreach reports a Farsi-language phishing campaign that exploited CVE-2021-40444 to deploy the PowerShortShell stealer, with almost half of victims in the US. SafeBreach describes its Telegram surveillance as typical of Infy, Ferocious Kitten and Rampant Kitten, without attributing the campaign to any of them.

campaigns.name: TAG-182 MarkiRAT distribution via fake apps
campaigns.summary: Recorded Future reports that the Iran-nexus cluster TAG-182 spread MarkiRAT through fake VPN and media-player apps, with tradecraft overlaps with Ferocious Kitten. The analysis cut-off is 2026-05-28.

diamond.adversary: Iran-based surveillance operators, named Ferocious Kitten by Kaspersky [S1]. The related TAG-182 cluster is assessed by Recorded Future as almost certainly part of Iran's state surveillance apparatus [S6].
diamond.capability: MarkiRAT Windows implant (keylogging, clipboard capture, file transfer, command execution); Telegram and Chrome launcher hijacking; trojanized Psiphon; BITSAdmin; macro-laden decoy documents; suspected Android implants [S1][S2][S4][S6][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: The same C2 domains were reused across implants for years [S1][S4], and APK/DEX files were hosted on C2 servers [S4]. In 2026, staged websites and Instagram posts pushed fake apps [S6].
diamond.victim: Persian-speaking individuals in Iran, especially people interested in protest or opposition content [S1][S2]. Per Recorded Future, the 2026 targets also include Iranians abroad [S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regime monitoring of dissent and of people who use circumvention tools to evade Iranian internet censorship [S2][S3][S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Telegram Desktop, Chrome and Psiphon, plus Android devices that sideload VPN or media apps from outside official stores [S2][S4][S6].

gaps: The primary Kaspersky Securelist report [S1] and the Recorded Future report/PDF [S6] could not be fetched (DNS blocked). Their details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
The Chinese intelligence firm that first analyzed the implant (mentioned in the imported summary) is not named in the sources gathered.

The CVE-2021-40444 / PowerShortShell link is unresolved. SOC Prime and Picus say Ferocious Kitten used CVE-2021-40444 [S9]. SafeBreach [S5] only compares the campaign's Telegram surveillance to Ferocious Kitten and others, without attribution.
The SafeBreach publication date (2021-11-24) comes from secondary coverage. The primary blog was not opened.

No Android Ferocious Kitten sample has been publicly confirmed. Kaspersky reported only indirect evidence [S4]. For TAG-182, secondary coverage differs on whether the Android apps carry MarkiRAT itself or whether the MarkiRAT seen is the Windows variant (e.g. 'svehost.exe'). Check against the primary report [S6].
No sponsoring Iranian organization (MOIS, IRGC or other) is named in the cited sources, and no government attribution or indictment was found.
Microsoft has no public name for this actor [S8].
Victim counts for the Kaspersky campaign are not available in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): The operational environment is personal Windows and Android devices of Persian-speaking users and the tools they rely on: Telegram, Chrome, Psiphon and sideloaded VPN or media apps [S2][S4][S6]. For DoD this matters mainly for personnel, partners, linguists or sources with Iranian ties, and for information-environment monitoring of Iranian domestic and diaspora populations. STEP 2 (effects): Iranian internet restrictions push targets toward circumvention tools, which the actor then trojanizes. Expect campaigns to follow censorship and connectivity events [S3][S6]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is a Persian-language lure (protest imagery or a fake VPN or media app), then macro or sideload execution, then MarkiRAT with BITS downloads, then persistence through Telegram or Chrome launcher hijacking, then collection of keystrokes, clipboard and files [S2][S6][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued surveillance of dissidents and diaspora through fake circumvention apps during unrest or after connectivity is restored [S6]. MDCOA is the same tooling turned against US-affiliated persons of Iranian heritage or partner-force personnel to collect contacts and credentials for counterintelligence targeting. That extension is an analytic inference not reported in the sources. Candidate indicators: BITS jobs pulling executables to user-writable paths; Telegram or Chrome shortcuts pointing to non-standard executables; Psiphon or 'Pis2ray'/'YEPlayer'/'YEMPlayer' binaries from unofficial sources; RTLO characters in attachment names; and macro-enabled Persian-language documents [S2][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: This actor targets individuals, not networks, so DODIN telemetry is unlikely to see it. Awareness depends on vendor reporting (Kaspersky, Recorded Future) and on Force Protection and counterintelligence channels [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: Activity against foreign nationals and diaspora falls mostly outside DoD cyber authorities. Coordinate with counterintelligence (AFOSI, DCSA) and with interagency partners for any US-person victims. (3) Mission assurance: Restrict sideloaded VPN and media apps on mobile devices used by linguists, partner liaisons and influence-operations personnel. Hunt for BITS abuse and Telegram/Chrome launcher tampering on any managed Windows endpoints [S6][S7]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators of fake circumvention apps with partners supporting Iranian information-environment operations, and track the unresolved TAG-182/Ferocious Kitten relationship rather than merging the clusters [S6].
